quote: Welches sind die invarianten Ungleichungen für [-..-] Realitätsfragen – entsprechend dem Cayley'schen Gedanken bei der binären Form 5ter Ordg.
english: What are the invariant inequalities for questions of reality, corresponding to Cayley's idea for the binary form of 5th order?
topic: Hilbert asks under what conditions real-valued invariants of forms come from forms with real coefficients, then reflects on logical rigour in mathematics and on judging branches of mathematics by their significance for the development of the human mind, citing Riemann and Cantor.

triage.modern_statement: Take a binary form f of degree n with real coefficients. Its roots can be real or come in complex-conjugate pairs, so its 'reality type' is the number of real roots and the number of conjugate pairs. The question is how to describe each reality type using only polynomial inequalities (sign conditions) on the SL2 invariants and covariants of f, so that the description does not depend on the choice of coordinates. Cayley and Sylvester had already done this for the quintic (n=5) using its invariants and the discriminant, and Hilbert asks how that generalises. A closely related question, from the page heading, is which real values of the invariants actually come from forms with real coefficients. In modern terms this means describing the real image of the invariant map (the real orbit space) as a semialgebraic set.
triage.answered_by: The quintic case that Hilbert treats as his model was settled in the 19th century: Sylvester gave invariant criteria for the reality of the roots of a quintic, and Cayley worked them out in his Eighth Memoir on Quantics (1858); Hermite also worked on this. For general degree, Hermite's method answers it in principle: the rank and signature of Hermite's quadratic form (or equivalently Sturm–Sylvester subresultant sign conditions) determine the number of real roots, and these expressions can be written in terms of invariants and covariants. Through Tarski–Seidenberg, every reality type is then a semialgebraic set. I did not find a source tying this specific diary note to a named later solution. I also did not find it among Hilbert's published problems, although it is thematically close to the real-algebraic questions in his 16th and 17th problems.

evidence.claim: Cayley's Eighth Memoir on Quantics applies the invariants of the binary quintic to the quintic and describes the basis of Sylvester's criteria for the reality of its roots, which is the 'Cayley idea' Hilbert refers to.

Hermite's theory: the rank and signature of Hermite's quadratic form determine the number of real roots. This is the general-degree tool for counting real roots through sign conditions on polynomial expressions in the coefficients.
Historical work on Cayley's and Harley's study of the quintic (1859–1863) uses semi-invariants and invariant-theory techniques.

Current research describes the space of real binary forms of a given degree as a finite union of semialgebraic sets, showing that semialgebraic descriptions of real binary forms are still studied today.

triage.why: The note is a brief, open-ended programme rather than a sharply stated conjecture. Its model case, the quintic, was already solved before Hilbert wrote it, and the general real-root question is solved in principle by Hermite/Sturm–Sylvester sign conditions and Tarski–Seidenberg, which is why I chose 'solved'. Two things I could not confirm, because my search budget ran out. First, a source showing that someone later produced a complete invariant-only system of inequalities for every degree. Second, a source covering the companion question of which real invariant values come from real forms; work on orbit-space inequalities by Procesi and Schwarz may be relevant but I could not check it. Semialgebraic studies of real binary forms continue today, but these sources do not show active work on this exact question, so 'active_today' is unclear and confidence is low.
